paras: The attempted lynching of Henry Forman was a gathering of a crowd at the jail in Helena, Montana Territory, on the night of December 22, 1882, aimed at hanging Forman, who was being held for shooting his son-in-law, Jacob Kenck. The crowd was persuaded to disperse, and Forman was later remanded to await the grand jury.

Kenck, a Helena brewer and saloon keeper, had married Forman's only daughter, who later died after an operation, and he had since remarried. According to the Butte Miner, Forman came to believe his daughter would still be alive had she not married Kenck, and this idea became a mania. The Helena Herald reported that Forman had threatened several times during the year to kill Kenck, but that the threats were taken as idle talk.

Shortly after noon on Friday, December 22, as Kenck stood in the doorway of the Helena Brewery saloon on upper Main street, Forman came up behind him and fired a revolver into his head. Wm. Steele followed Forman out the back of the saloon and arrested him, and Forman, speaking in 'broken English,' gave himself up and handed over the revolver. Kenck died at about a quarter to seven that evening.

The same day, the Helena Herald wrote that Kenck's fellow citizens were 'loud in their cries for immediate vengeance' and that it was undetermined whether the law would be allowed to take its course. In jail, according to the New North-West, Forman was told Kenck's friends might hang him and replied that, if so, he wanted 'three Germans to hang him at his own cabin.' That night, about 1 o'clock by the Billings Herald's account, a crowd gathered in front of the jail with the aim of taking 'summary vengeance,' and the Butte Miner said an attempt was made to organize a lynching party. The New North-West reported that the jail guard had been 'strongly re-enforced' but was never tested, because 'wiser counsel prevailed' and the men went away.

Forman appeared before Probate Judge Sterling, waived examination, and was remanded to jail without bail to await the next Territorial Grand Jury. No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage, and no one in the crowd was reported arrested.

Montana papers carried the killing widely, from a Helena dispatch in the Butte Miner of December 23 to briefs in the Billings Herald and the Rocky Mountain Husbandman and a longer article in the Deer Lodge New North-West. Their focus was Kenck's death and Forman's mind; the jail crowd appeared only in a closing sentence, and each paper credited 'good counsels' or 'more reasonable citizens' for ending it. None of the reports gave a race for Forman or for the crowd.

The Helena Herald called Forman a 'crazy assassin' and used its editorial 'Cranks' to urge that demented men be confined and pistol sales regulated. The New North-West, writing 'as a friend of the murdered man,' judged Forman insane, called the act 'a misfortune, not a crime,' and compared him with Guiteau.

Forman's first name appears as Henry in most reports, as 'W. S.' in the first Miner dispatch and the Husbandman, and as 'Fred' in an eyewitness statement quoted by the Helena Herald. The Husbandman dated the shooting Friday, December 23, while the other reports and the Helena dispatch place it on the 22nd.

bases: A crowd gathered at the Helena jail with talk of taking out and hanging a prisoner held for murder, then dispersed without violence (A2, A3, A8).

No one was killed: a crowd that gathered at the jail intending to hang Forman for the killing of Jacob Kenck was persuaded to disperse and the guard was never tested (A2, A3, A8); it was a threatened or attempted lynching only.
Three papers (Butte, Billings, Deer Lodge) independently report the crowd at the jail and its dispersal (A2, A3, A8).

accounts.label: Butte Miner
accounts.gist: After Kenck died, excited men gathered at the jail and tried to organize a lynching party, but good counsels prevailed and they dispersed quietly.

accounts.label: Billings Herald brief
accounts.gist: About 1 o'clock that night a crowd gathered in front of the jail to take 'summary vengeance' but was talked out of it by more reasonable citizens.

accounts.label: New North-West (Deer Lodge)
accounts.gist: A large number of men gathered around the jail with an apparent disposition to take Forman out and hang him; wiser counsel prevailed and the reinforced guard was not tested.

accounts.label: Helena Daily Herald (same day)
accounts.gist: Before the crowd gathered, reported citizens 'loud in their cries for immediate vengeance' and left open whether the law would take its course.

framing.detail: The Helena Herald called Forman a 'cowardly' and 'crazy assassin' and reported calls for 'immediate vengeance' without condemning them, while its editorial 'Cranks' urged asylum confinement and pistol laws instead.
The Miner, Billings Herald and New North-West reported the jail crowd in a closing sentence and credited 'good counsels' and 'more reasonable citizens' for its dispersal.
The New North-West ('A Distressing Tragedy') argued Forman was insane, that his act was 'a misfortune, not a crime', and that the insane should be confined.

conflicts.note: Most reports, including the Helena Herald's court item, give Henry.
The Dec. 22 dispatch dateline and most reports give the 22d; the Husbandman's 23d appears to be an error.
Minor; the local Helena account says just after noon.
